What the LDM-RL measurements actually support¶

2026-09-04. GRPO fine-tuning of a Qwen3.5-9B hybrid (Gated DeltaNet linear attention, full attention at layers 3, 7, …, 31) for molecular acquisition-function optimisation, with a Qwen2.5-1.5B control that trains cleanly. Five adversarial reviews of the campaign's own records ran against this notebook's inputs; four of the five load-bearing conclusions did not survive, and the one new positive result below was already in the logs, uncounted.

Every figure reads results/session_20260904.json, extracted once from the run logs, so a figure and the sentence beside it cannot disagree.

In [1]:

1. The reward cannot measure policy quality¶

The campaign's headline negative result was "raw_reward fell from 0.0172 to 0.0023 across a completed run, so the policy got worse." The reward is expected hypervolume improvement against an evolving Pareto front scored by a growing GP. It is a shrinking ruler.

The left panel isolates the ruler from the policy: hold a set of molecules fixed and vary only the GP history. The right panel replaces the ruler and re-measures 40 real runs.

The decline belongs to the ruler. With the molecules genuinely held fixed and only the GP history varying, the reward as used falls to exactly zero while the frozen-GP yardstick does not move at all (spread 0.000 across every history size). Re-measuring 40 real runs with both rulers: raw_reward declines in 36 of 40 (sign test p = 2e-07, mean rank correlation with time −0.57 ± 0.05), the frozen yardstick in 22 of 40 — a coin flip (p = 0.64, ρ = +0.01 ± 0.05).

One correction to this notebook's own earlier evidence. The first version of this section said "the same eight held-out candidates". It was not: probe_acq_reward.py:44 slices rows_all[N_HIST : N_HIST+8], so the candidate set moved with the history size. The conclusion survives re-testing with the molecules actually fixed, and the numbers above are from that re-test — but the original figure was measuring two things changing at once.

Retracted. raw_reward carries no information about policy quality; no statement about whether this pipeline learns has ever been testable with it. The yardstick separates the extremes (top-20 vs bottom-20 molecules realise hypervolume gain 0.027 vs exactly 0) and ranks the middle weakly — Spearman +0.13 against realised gain — so it is a comparative instrument, not a calibrated predictor.

2. The zero-variance rate is a function of where you stop looking¶

Zero-variance rollouts (all trajectories in a group score identically) produce no gradient, so their rate is the campaign's main outcome measure. Runs die at different lengths, and the rate drifts within a run — so a cell's number depends on how long its runs happened to survive.

At a common cut the two n=4 cells are indistinguishable, while the published table reported the acquisition/ΔHV ratio there as 5.19×. That ratio compared cells measured at 60, 22, 52 and 133 rounds.

The group-size effect does not survive the same treatment either, and this figure is where that became visible. An earlier draft of this section said the n=2 versus n=4 gap "is present at every depth". It is not: at the shallowest cut the ordering reverses. The reason is mechanical — the shallow row is dominated by runs that have only just started, and the zero-variance rate is high in a run's opening rounds while the GP is still cold. So the shallow cut compares maturity, not configuration, and the deeper cuts have one or two runs per cell with a within-cell spread as large as the means.

The refill is still in flight. The honest reading today is that no cell contrast in this matrix is established, and the curve is published in this state on purpose: a single number would have concealed both the reversal and the fact that its own truncation point is what produced it.

And the replicates are not replicates¶

The shared checkout was edited while the matrix was filling: bridge.py at 14:58, arguments.py at 15:01, the loss and the launchers at 15:11 -- and the runs started between 15:03 and 15:13. Stamping each run directory with a hash of the files it actually loaded gives:

cell runs code states
acq_n2 4 2
acq_n4 7 3
dhv_n2 5 3
dhv_n4 5 2

Every cell is mixed, and seven runs carry no stamp at all because they predate the stamping. Two runs in one cell that loaded different code are not replicates, so the within-cell spread this matrix reports is not the noise floor -- it is noise plus an unmeasured code difference, and it understates the true uncertainty rather than overstating it.

This is the same defect as the ones above wearing different clothes: a value that changed without being recorded. The launcher now stamps the fingerprint into every run directory, so future pools can be split by code state instead of assumed homogeneous; the runs already on disk cannot be repaired, only labelled.

3. The group-size cell was also getting twice the training¶

launchers/run_train_real_slime_param.sh hard-coded --global-batch-size 2 while --n-samples-per-prompt was the knob under study. Optimiser steps per round = rollout_batch × n_samples ÷ global_batch, so the knob moved the training budget too.

The n=4 cells received exactly twice the gradient updates of the n=2 cells at the same round count, so "group size is an effective knob" was never separated from "twice the training". On the 9B side the two configuration files both labelled n4 differ four-fold on the same axis.

Fixed: the launcher now declares UPDATES_PER_ROLLOUT, derives global_batch from it, asserts divisibility, and prints the resolved triple — the pattern this repo's own conventions already mandate elsewhere and which this line had never applied.

4. The 9B and 1.5B gradient distributions do not overlap¶

In [5]:

print(f"9B    min {g9.min():.4g}  median {np.median(g9):.4g}  max {g9.max():.4g}")

1.5B  min 0.006474  median 5.857  max 1.655e+05
9B    min 2.467e+07  median 7.857e+08  max 2.064e+12
separation: 9B minimum is 149x the 1.5B maximum

No 9B step has ever produced a gradient within five orders of magnitude of the healthy scale. The distributions are disjoint: the smallest 9B gradient exceeds the largest 1.5B gradient by two orders. Since clip_grad = 1.0 rescales by a positive scalar, the direction is preserved exactly — so "the direction is noise" was never shown. What the data does support is concentration: with one tensor at ~1e8 and the output layer at ~2e-2, after clipping to unit norm most parameters receive an update of order 1e-9 of nominal, making the update effectively rank-few.

5. The nan boundary lands on a full-attention layer, 64 times out of 64¶

The backward pass runs layer 31 → 0, so the largest contaminated layer index is where the non-finite value first appears. The published table gave one such index per run and built a between-run contrast on it. Each run in fact emits ten reports per rank, and the index varies within every run — so the contrast was an artefact of which line was tabulated. Counting all of them gives a much stronger result than the one that was reported.

In [6]:

observed boundary layers: {19: 2, 23: 2, 27: 22, 31: 38}
full-attention layers   : [3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 27, 31]
on a full-attention layer: 64/64
uniform-null p, counting only the 4 distinct values: 0.0039

The nan is created inside a full-attention layer's backward, not in the Gated DeltaNet. Under a uniform boundary the probability of landing in the 8-layer full-attention set is 1/4; even counting only the four distinct observed values as independent, p = 0.004.

This overturns the campaign's own reasoning twice over. The earlier conclusion blamed the GDN because linear_attn.A_log and dt_bias were nan in every report — but those are nan precisely because they sit downstream in the backward, i.e. they are the most conspicuous members of the set "everything already contaminated". A parameter that is always nan carries the least information. The later conclusion then read full_attention_interval: 4 as layers {0, 4, …, 28} when the actual set is {3, 7, …, 31}, which misfiled the wavefront layer 28 — a GDN layer, and the last clean one — as full attention. The right answer was reachable from the same logs by counting instead of reading one line each.

6. What the design can and cannot resolve¶

In [7]:
# The pooled within-cell SD is computed from matrix_2x2.json, not written in.
# An earlier draft hard-coded s = 0.0958 here. That number came from a smaller
# snapshot, and by the time the matrix filled it was 7.8x too small on the metric
# the panel actually plots -- which turned an unresolvable comparison into an
# apparently easy one. The docstring at the top of this builder says the notebook
# reads matrix_2x2.json directly "so a figure and the prose beside it cannot
# disagree"; a baked-in constant is exactly the thing that defeats that.

def pooled_sd(key):
    v = [C_[key + "_sd"]**2 for C_ in mx["cells"].values() if C_.get(key + "_sd") is not None]
    return float(np.sqrt(np.mean(v)))

def main_effects(key):
    g = {k: mx["cells"][k][key + "_rate"] for k in mx["cells"]}
    reward = abs(np.mean([g["acq_n2"], g["acq_n4"]]) - np.mean([g["dhv_n2"], g["dhv_n4"]]))
    group  = abs(np.mean([g["acq_n2"], g["dhv_n2"]]) - np.mean([g["acq_n4"], g["dhv_n4"]]))
    return reward, group

z = 2.802                     # z(.975) + z(.80)
METRICS = [("zs",    "zero-variance groups per round"),
           ("below", "degenerate steps per run")]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.2, 2.9))
for ax, (key, label) in zip(axes, METRICS):
    s_ = pooled_sd(key)
    eff = np.linspace(0.02, 0.62, 400)
    ax.plot(eff, (z*s_/eff)**2, color=INK, lw=1.6)
    ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_ylim(0.5, 3e4)
    ax.set_xlabel(f"true main effect ({label})")
    ax.set_ylabel("runs per cell for 80% power")
    r_eff, g_eff = main_effects(key)
    for x, lab, col in [(r_eff, "reward form", HL), (g_eff, "group size", OK)]:
        if x <= 0.005:
            continue
        n = (z*s_/x)**2
        ax.plot([x], [n], "o", color=col, ms=6)
        ax.annotate(f"{lab}\n{n:.0f}/cell", (x, n), textcoords="offset points",
                    xytext=(7, 5), fontsize=6.5, color=col)
    ax.axhline(5.25, color=MUTE, ls="--", lw=1.1)
    ax.annotate("this design (~5 runs/cell)", (0.30, 6.4), fontsize=6.5, color=MUTE)
    ax.set_title(f"{label}\npooled within-cell SD = {s_:.3f}", fontsize=8)
fig.suptitle("The same runs answer one metric and cannot answer the other", fontsize=9)
show(fig)

for key, label in METRICS:
    s_ = pooled_sd(key); r_eff, g_eff = main_effects(key)
    print(f"{label}:  pooled within-cell SD = {s_:.4f}")
    for x, lab in [(r_eff, "reward form"), (g_eff, "group size")]:
        need = float("inf") if x <= 0.005 else (z*s_/x)**2
        print(f"    {lab:12} effect {x:.3f} -> {need:8.1f} runs/cell")

    reward form  effect 0.017 ->  10249.3 runs/cell
    group size   effect 0.131 ->    173.1 runs/cell

The reward-form contrast needs about 16 runs per cell and the design has ~3.5. Achieved power against the observed effect is 21%; the effect (+0.07, CI spanning zero, p = 0.20) is smaller than the run-to-run scatter within a single cell.

The group-size effect looked like the one contrast this design could resolve. §6b shows that about two thirds of it is the metric's own arithmetic, and that what remains exists on only one of the two objectives. The power curve above is computed on the raw scale, so the point it marks "group size" is measuring the exponent as much as the treatment. What the power curve establishes is a lower bound on the design, not a licence for the one contrast that happened to clear it. An effect estimated from the same small sample that the power calculation is run on is systematically the optimistic end of its own interval, which is the failure this campaign has already recorded three times.

6b. Two thirds of the group-size effect is the metric's own arithmetic¶

zero_std counts the groups whose n rewards are all exactly equal. Under any exchangeable model that probability falls with n by construction, so comparing the raw rate between the n=2 and the n=4 cells measures the exponent as much as it measures the treatment. The mechanism offered for the effect — more samples per group, less chance every reward ties — is the null hypothesis, not an explanation of a departure from it.

The fix is to compare on a per-sample scale, q = p^(1/n), where "no effect" means "no difference". Two further corrections are applied here: nine runs actually ran n_samples_per_prompt = 1 (read from each train.log's argv, not from the run name) and cannot produce a gradient at all, and the panel is repeated inside the single code state that removes the checkout-drift confound.

import glob, re
from pathlib import Path as _P

NOM = {"acq_n2": 2, "acq_n4": 4, "dhv_n2": 2, "dhv_n4": 4}
_PATS = {"acq_n2": ("runs/M-acqn2-*", "runs/X-acqn2-*"), "acq_n4": ("runs/M-acqn4-*", "runs/X-acqn4-*"),
         "dhv_n2": ("runs/M-dhvn2-*", "runs/X-dhvn2-*"), "dhv_n4": ("runs/M-dhvn4-*", "runs/X-dhvn4-*")}
_ROOT = _P("/lus/lfs1aip2/projects/public/u6gb/tasks/large-discovery-model/ldm_rl")

# The nominal n is in the run's NAME; the n it actually ran is in its argv. They disagree
# for nine runs, and the collector filters on neither.
_meta = {}
for _ps in _PATS.values():
    for _pat in _ps:
        for _ds in glob.glob(str(_ROOT / _pat)):
            _d = _P(_ds); _k = _d.name.rsplit("_", 1)[0]
            _fp = _d / "code_fingerprint.txt"; _lg = _d / "train.log"
            _n = None
            if _lg.exists():
                _m = re.search(r'--n-samples-per-prompt\s+(\d+)', _lg.read_text(errors="replace")[:400000])
                if _m: _n = int(_m.group(1))
            _meta[_k] = (_fp.read_text().strip() if _fp.exists() else "unstamped", _n)

_STAMP = "3084d1972608"
def _rows(cell, clean):
    out = []
    for r in mx["cells"][cell]["per_run"]:
        st, n = _meta.get(r["run"], ("unstamped", None))
        if n != NOM[cell]:                      # drops the n=1 runs
            continue
        if clean and st != _STAMP:
            continue
        out.append(r["zs_rate"])
    return np.array(out, float)

def _welch(a, b):
    va, vb = a.var(ddof=1)/len(a), b.var(ddof=1)/len(b)
    se = np.sqrt(va + vb)
    return (a.mean() - b.mean())/se if se > 0 else np.nan

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.2, 3.1))
for ax, (clean, title) in zip(axes, [(False, "all runs with the correct n"),
                                     (True, "single code state, correct n")]):
    P_ = {c: _rows(c, clean) for c in NOM}
    Q_ = {c: P_[c] ** (1.0/NOM[c]) for c in NOM}
    _xs = np.arange(2); _bw = 0.36
    for _off, _D, _lab, _col in [(-_bw/2, P_, "raw  p", HL), (_bw/2, Q_, "per-sample  q", OK)]:
        for i, ep in enumerate(("acq", "dhv")):
            _diff = _D[ep+"_n2"].mean() - _D[ep+"_n4"].mean()
            _t = _welch(_D[ep+"_n2"], _D[ep+"_n4"])
            ax.bar(i+_off, _diff, _bw, color=_col, alpha=.85,
                   label=_lab if i == 0 else None)
            ax.annotate(f"t={_t:+.2f}", (i+_off, _diff), ha="center", va="bottom",
                        fontsize=6.5, color=_col,
                        xytext=(0, 2), textcoords="offset points")
    ax.axhline(0, color=INK, lw=.8)
    ax.set_xticks(_xs); ax.set_xticklabels(["acq  (acquisition)", "dhv  (hypervolume)"])
    ax.set_ylabel("n=2 minus n=4  (zero-variance rate)")
    ax.set_title(title + f"\nn per cell: " + "/".join(str(len(_rows(c, clean))) for c in NOM), fontsize=8)
    ax.legend(fontsize=6.5, frameon=False)
fig.suptitle("On a per-sample scale the group-size effect exists on one objective only", fontsize=9)
show(fig)

for clean, title in [(False, "all runs with the correct n"), (True, "single code state, correct n")]:
    P_ = {c: _rows(c, clean) for c in NOM}
    Q_ = {c: P_[c] ** (1.0/NOM[c]) for c in NOM}
    n2p = np.concatenate([P_["acq_n2"], P_["dhv_n2"]]); n4p = np.concatenate([P_["acq_n4"], P_["dhv_n4"]])
    n2q = np.concatenate([Q_["acq_n2"], Q_["dhv_n2"]]); n4q = np.concatenate([Q_["acq_n4"], Q_["dhv_n4"]])
    qbar = np.mean([Q_["acq_n2"].mean(), Q_["dhv_n2"].mean()])
    pred = qbar**2 - qbar**4; obs = n2p.mean() - n4p.mean()
    print(f"{title}   (n per cell: " + "/".join(str(len(P_[c])) for c in NOM) + ")")
    print(f"    raw scale p : diff {obs:+.4f}  t={_welch(n2p, n4p):+.2f}")
    print(f"    per-sample q: diff {n2q.mean()-n4q.mean():+.4f}  t={_welch(n2q, n4q):+.2f}")
    for ep in ("acq", "dhv"):
        print(f"        {ep} on q: diff {Q_[ep+'_n2'].mean()-Q_[ep+'_n4'].mean():+.4f}  t={_welch(Q_[ep+'_n2'], Q_[ep+'_n4']):+.2f}")
    print(f"    arithmetic-only prediction (q={qbar:.4f} fixed): {pred:+.4f}  = {pred/obs*100:.0f}% of the raw effect\n")

The raw effect is +0.35 and the arithmetic alone predicts +0.24 of it. What survives on the per-sample scale does not survive equally: on the acquisition objective the group-size difference is +0.07 (t = +0.99, single code state), which is nothing, while on the hypervolume objective it is +0.44 (t = +3.91). The "consistent direction across both objectives" that made the earlier reading persuasive was supplied by the exponent, and once the exponent is removed the effect lives on one objective only.

Two consequences. The comparison to report is per objective, not pooled. And a rate compared across groups of different size needs the value its own arithmetic predicts under no effect computed before the difference is interpreted — the same check would have caught this in seconds at any point in the past two days.

6c. What one frozen-policy run does and does not establish¶

Section 1 shows the docking objective getting worse within a run, and nothing in the campaign could say whether that was the policy learning something harmful or the acquisition process saturating on its own: no run had ever been executed with learning switched off. LR0-20260905T034032Z is that run — identical to a dhv / n=4 cell in every argument except --lr 0 --weight-decay 0. It completed all 50 steps and 842 proposals.

The learning rate took effect at the level of the saved parameters, which is a stronger statement than "it was passed". Comparing ckpt/iter_0000009 against ckpt/iter_0000019 through the checkpoint metadata's byte offsets, all 226 model parameters are byte-identical across 2,944.8 MiB, while 397 of 597 optimizer tensors differ.

The 227th entry in the parameter-class group is rng_state/shard_0.0_1.1, 15,449 bytes, and it does differ. It is not a model parameter: it is the RNG state, which advances whenever random numbers are drawn and would therefore differ between any two checkpoints regardless of the learning rate. It does affect the function in the sense that sampling is stochastic, but it carries no learned information and its change is not evidence that weights moved. (An earlier version of this section wrote "226 of 227 parameter tensors", which put a non-parameter in the denominator.)

Why the weights could not have moved, argued forward from the configuration rather than backward from the checkpoints. The resolved argument dump in the run's own log records:

lr = 0.0     min_lr = 0.0     lr_decay_style = constant     lr_warmup_iters = 0

optimizer_param_scheduler.py:269 rewrites param_group['lr'] = self.get_lr(param_group) on every step, and under constant decay get_lr is bounded by max_lr and min_lr, both of which are 0.0 here (the scheduler's constructor asserts max_lr >= min_lr, and both ends are zero). Adam's update is param -= lr * step, so the displacement is identically zero at every step regardless of what the gradient was. The byte-identical parameters are the prediction this makes, confirmed — not the premise it is inferred from.

The optimizer state moving is the same argument's other half: Adam's exp_avg and exp_avg_sq are functions of the gradient alone and do not contain lr, so they advance while the parameters do not. Both halves follow from the update rule; neither needs an elimination over alternatives.

For completeness, the run also did not skip steps (skipped_train_samples = 0, train/step advancing 0→99) and its gradients were not degenerate (grad_norm min 0.0349, median 5.64, max 3586.6). Those are consistency checks on the above, not the argument.

What that licenses is narrow. Frozen weights showing the same decline establishes that a change in weights is not necessary for the decline to appear. It does not establish that weight change contributes nothing when it does occur, and it does not make the two conditions equivalent.

Three verdicts, kept separate¶

Supported. The learning rate reached the optimizer and the weights did not move: 226/227 parameter tensors byte-identical across 2,944.8 MiB while 397/597 optimizer tensors changed. And a change in weights is not necessary for the decline: with the policy frozen the objective still fails to improve at every prefix length tested.

Refuted — an earlier claim in this notebook's own history. A previous version compared the control's rho over all 842 of its proposals against the pooled mean of 58 runs from all four cells, and read it as ruling out RL as the main cause. That comparison was wrong in three ways. It pooled across objectives and group sizes when only dhv / n=4 is comparable. It did not match length, and length matters: the pooled mean of +0.074 falls to +0.005 at a 150-proposal prefix. And it judged a single run against the confidence interval for a mean, which is the wrong interval — the right one is the prediction interval for a new run, about 3x wider here. Matched properly, the control sits outside the mean CI at K=150 and swings between -0.220 and +0.153 across prefixes.

Underpowered, and this is the honest state. The control lands inside the prediction interval at all 11 prefix lengths, but those intervals span roughly ±0.2 to ±0.75 — they would accommodate almost any result, so "inside" carries little information. Formally, the narrowest equivalence margin one control run can support is wider than the effect being tested at every length: |delta| < 0.353 at K=150 against a training mean of 0.005, |delta| < 0.129 at K=400 against 0.029. A non-significant difference is not equivalence, and here the data cannot support an equivalence claim at any margin that would be interesting. Nothing about the acquisition objective or about n=2 is touched at all.

6d. The sample size depends on a prefix that was chosen after seeing the data¶

Section 6c compares runs at a matched prefix K. The number of runs a follow-up needs depends on the run-to-run SD at that K — and that SD does not fall monotonically with K. It oscillates, so a K picked after looking at the data can make the same design appear to cost anywhere from 2 runs per arm to 37.

The earlier figure of "5 per arm, 3 more runs" was wrong twice. The prefix K=400 sits in a trough of the SD curve and was selected after seeing the data — at K=250 the same calculation demands 19 per arm, at K=100 it demands 37. And the arithmetic subtracted the shortfall from the wrong arm: at K=400 the trained arm has 7 qualifying runs and the control arm has 1, so reaching 5 per arm needs 4 more controls, not 3.

The only choice of K that is genuinely free of hindsight is the length every run shares, which here is 8 proposals — and there the SD is 0.38 and the design would need 229 runs per arm. That is not a usable design; it is a demonstration that this metric does not settle down until several hundred proposals in.

What was done instead, and exactly how far it goes. K, the inclusion rule, the minimum effect of interest and the equivalence margin are written down in plan/PRESPEC_lr0_control.md and were frozen before the second control run started.

That document is prospective for the four new control runs and for nothing else. The trained arm already existed and was inspected while K and the sizing SD were being chosen — K=400 was selected from an SD curve computed on those very runs. So the comparison is one arm collected under fixed rules against one arm that was not, and its overall type-I error is not controlled at the nominal 0.05. It is weaker than a pre-registered two-arm trial and is not reported as one.

The SD used for sizing is a prior from 7 trained runs, not a fact about the control arm. The analysis re-estimates it from the completed arms and reports whatever resolvable |delta| is actually achieved; if that SD comes out materially larger, the report is "underpowered at the frozen margin", not a new sample size chosen to fit.

6e. The control arm, harvested under the frozen rules¶

All five control attempts are resolved. This is the current and only result.

value
control arm 4 of 5 attempts qualified (LR0c4 failed on CUDA OOM at 11 proposals)
reaching K 7/20 trained against 4/5 control, Fisher p = 0.133
difference trained +0.0286 (n=7) against control +0.0946 (n=4); diff −0.0660, 95% CI [−0.1475, +0.0155], p = 0.0961 — not detected
equivalence not established; see the direction note below
power underpowered at the frozen margin; resolvable |delta| = 0.108 against 0.10
budget 21.93 GPU-hours of 27.5 authorised

The TOST directions, read off the producer rather than paraphrased. harvest_lr0_arm.py defines diff = trained_mean − control_mean = −0.0660, and at lines 132–133 tl = (diff + DELTA)/se, tu = (DELTA − diff)/se. So:

  • upper p = 0.0011 tests H0: diff >= +0.10, i.e. the trained arm exceeds the control by 0.10 or more. Rejected → the trained arm is not higher than the control by 0.10.
  • lower p = 0.176 tests H0: diff <= −0.10, i.e. the trained arm falls below the control by 0.10 or more. Not rejected → that cannot be excluded.

An earlier version of this text stated both sides the other way round, which turned the side that failed into the side that held. The asymmetry matters: the control mean (+0.095) sits above the trained mean (+0.029), so "trained far above control" is easy to exclude while "control far above trained" is not — and it is the second that bears on whether training is harmful.

plan/harvest_lr0_arm.py applies the frozen rules — K=400, warm-start 63 dropped, argv n_samples == 4 — and reports difference, equivalence and power as three separate verdicts, recording why each excluded run was excluded rather than dropping it silently. The cell below re-runs it against the live run directories, so the table above and the output below are produced by the same code path.

In [11]:
# Provenance and failure handling. The first version of this cell ran an absolute path
# outside the repository and printed only stdout, so a non-zero exit or a traceback on
# stderr would have left an empty-looking but GREEN cell -- the notebook would publish as
# if acceptance had passed. Three changes:
#   1. prefer the copy published alongside this notebook, so the producer travels with it
#      and a reader is not depending on a file that only exists on one filesystem;
#   2. surface returncode and stderr, and raise on failure so the cell goes red;
#   3. print the producer's own identity and the identity of the data it read.
import subprocess as _sub, hashlib as _hl, os as _os
from pathlib import Path as _Pp

_HERE = _Pp.cwd()
_CANDIDATES = [_HERE/"harvest_lr0_arm.py",                    # published beside this notebook
               _HERE/"rl"/"slime_launch"/"harvest_lr0_arm.py",
               _Pp("/lus/lfs1aip2/projects/public/u6gb/tasks/large-discovery-model/ldm_rl/plan/harvest_lr0_arm.py")]
_PROD = next((c for c in _CANDIDATES if c.exists()), None)
if _PROD is None:
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"harvest producer not found in any of {[str(c) for c in _CANDIDATES]}")

_src = _PROD.read_bytes()
print(f"producer : {_PROD}")
print(f"           sha256 {_hl.sha256(_src).hexdigest()[:16]}  {len(_src)} bytes")

_RUNS = _Pp("/lus/lfs1aip2/projects/public/u6gb/tasks/large-discovery-model/ldm_rl/runs")
print(f"data root: {_RUNS}  (exists={_RUNS.exists()})")
try:
    _rev = _sub.run(["git","rev-parse","--short","HEAD"], capture_output=True, text=True,
                    timeout=60, cwd=str(_HERE)).stdout.strip()
    _dirty = _sub.run(["git","status","--porcelain","--","."], capture_output=True, text=True,
                      timeout=60, cwd=str(_HERE)).stdout.strip()
    print(f"repo     : {_rev or 'unknown'}{' (working tree dirty)' if _dirty else ''}")
except Exception as _e:
    print(f"repo     : unavailable ({type(_e).__name__})")

_r = _sub.run(["python3", str(_PROD)], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=1800)
print(f"exit     : {_r.returncode}")
print("-"*76)
print(_r.stdout)
if _r.stderr.strip():
    print("-"*76 + "\nSTDERR:\n" + _r.stderr)
if _r.returncode != 0:
    raise RuntimeError(f"harvest producer exited {_r.returncode}; acceptance is NOT valid. "
                       f"stderr tail: {_r.stderr.strip()[-500:]}")
# Checking only the first heading accepts a producer that prints "1. DIFFERENCE" and then
# dies before EQUIVALENCE or POWER, with rc=0. A supervisor's counter-example did exactly
# that. Require every section AND the numeric field each one must carry, so a heading with
# no result underneath is caught too.
_REQUIRED = [
    ("INCLUSION CENSUS", ["reaching K:"]),
    ("1. DIFFERENCE",    ["trained mean", "control mean", "diff ", "95% CI", "->"]),
    ("2. EQUIVALENCE",   ["lower p=", "upper p=", "->"]),
    ("3. POWER",         ["pooled sd", "resolvable |delta|", "->"]),
]
_missing = []
for _sec, _fields in _REQUIRED:
    if _sec not in _r.stdout:
        _missing.append(f"section '{_sec}'"); continue
    _tail = _r.stdout.split(_sec, 1)[1]
    _stop = min([_tail.find(x) for x, _ in _REQUIRED if x in _tail and _tail.find(x) > 0] or [len(_tail)])
    _body = _tail[:_stop]
    for _f in _fields:
        if _f not in _body:
            _missing.append(f"'{_f}' under '{_sec}'")
if _missing:
    raise RuntimeError("harvest output is incomplete and must not be read as an acceptance "
                       f"result. Missing: {_missing}")
print(f"completeness: all {len(_REQUIRED)} sections present with their required fields")

The inclusion rule carries a selection effect, and it is stronger than "both arms get the same rule".

arm directories no gp_history argv n != 4 shorter than K qualifying reached K
trained, lr=1e-6 25 0 5 13 7 35.0%
control, lr=0 5 0 0 1 4 80%

Both arms are collected under the same rule, so the comparison stays like-for-like. Withdrawn. Reaching 400 proposals is a post-treatment variable. If the learning rate influences whether a run gets there, conditioning on >= 400 selects a different sub-population within each arm, and applying an identical rule to both does not restore exchangeability — the criterion is downstream of the treatment, so the filter is part of what the treatment did.

Fisher exact on 7/20 against 4/5 gives p = 0.133. That is not evidence of no difference: with five control attempts the test has very little power, while the point estimates are 35% against 80%. Pre-filter proposal counts are [0,0,0,0,0,0,0,8,20,61,177, 253,285,426,493,501,574,588,619,654] for the trained arm against [11,404,670,685,842] for the control — the 11 is LR0c4, which died of CUDA OOM and is kept in the denominator because removing a failure by its cause is selecting on the outcome.

And narrowing the stated population does not repair the comparison. Filtering each arm to >= 400 does not give one population seen under two treatments; it gives two different populations, each selected by a criterion the treatment may itself have moved. "Runs that reached 400 proposals under lr=0" and "runs that reached 400 proposals under lr=1e-6" are not the same set of runs, and no relabelling makes them one.

What this design can report is therefore descriptive: the difference between two observed, conditionally-selected groups. It is not a treatment effect on a common population and is not written as one anywhere below — the phrasing is "the observed difference between the qualifying groups", never "the effect of lr=0". Recovering a causal contrast would need an outcome defined on every run regardless of length, so that nothing is conditioned away, or a completion model that is itself identified. This design has neither. K is not re-chosen after the fact, and the completion rates travel with every number quoted.

7. A quarter of the campaign's rounds were recorded as never having happened¶

The launcher put the > train.log redirect outside the bash -lc "…" quote, so the file held the stream the login-node srun client received. Losing the login side stopped the file while the compute node carried on.

11 runs with truncated logs: 150 rounds recorded -> 320 actually run
  gp_grew_but_no_round_was_ever_logged: 13

163 recorded rounds were actually 333, across 20 truncated logs, in two mass events (2026-09-04 13:52–13:53 and 2026-09-02 08:20–08:22) plus nine singles. Rounds were proven from ckpt/latest_checkpointed_iteration.txt, with the checkpoint-to-round offset verified against a run whose log is intact rather than assumed; the rule that a COMPLETED run did num_rollout rounds holds in 24 of 24 intact-log cases. One run previously classified never_started had completed all 30.

Two consequences beyond the count. First, 29 runs move from "failed for an unknown reason" to "completed" — "no error string in the log" was being read as an unexplained failure when it often meant the log stopped early. Second, and worse for the 2×2: the truncation lands at one wall-clock instant while cells run at different speeds (n=4 takes 102–142 s per round, n=2 57–73 s), so the slower cells lose systematically more rounds, and any filter of the form "runs that reached round N" excludes runs in a cell-dependent way. The matrix collector now separates censored by log truncation from genuinely stopped at every cut.

What is not recoverable: the per-round data for those 170 rounds — zero_std, raw_reward, grad_norm — exists nowhere on disk. The recovery fixes denominators and eligibility, never numerators. GP-row growth proves a run kept working and bounds rounds from below, but it cannot be inverted into a round count: rows per round is a random variable (how many proposals parsed into an evaluable molecule), ±16% within one cell at best and over 100% across the population.

8. The out-of-memory failures were one missing subtraction¶

96 runs died out of memory. 62 of them allocate a tensor whose size resolves exactly to [T_padded, 151936] × 4 bytes — the fp32 logits — at three separate lines. The interesting quantity is therefore not the memory but T, the tokens in one micro-batch.

  12.90 GiB -> T =  22784  = 2.78x the cap

The cap was set to a value a valid sample must exceed. --max-tokens-per-gpu was set equal to --rollout-max-response-len (both 8192), but the prompt is a constant 340 tokens, so a maximally-truncated sample is 8532 — structurally one prompt over the cap, every time. That alone accounts for the modal 4.86 GiB failure and needs no unusual behaviour at all. The launcher now derives the cap from response_len + prompt_headroom; declaring the two independently is what let them drift into an impossible relation.

The large ones are a missing subtraction. ldm_rl.bridge.generate loops over spec.iterations = 20 turns and passes the same sampling_params on every turn, so each turn is granted the full 8192 new tokens and the environment observations are appended with no budget check — a ceiling near 164k tokens in a single training sample. Upstream slime does exactly the missing line: sampling_params["max_new_tokens"] -= sample.response_length. The packer was never at fault; it enforces its bound correctly and simply cannot split one sample, so an over-cap sample lands alone in its bin — the documented exception, silently accepted.

The 22,784-token micro-batch was reconstructed from the log alone before the fix: for one rollout, sum(total_lengths) = 26,565 across 3 micro-batches, while three legal micro-batches could hold at most 25,596 — so at least one sample had to be over-cap, and lengths [22784, 1240, 1250, 1291] reproduce all four logged quantities at once.

Two further findings without which the arithmetic does not close: slime's chunked log-prob implementation already existed and was simply defaulted off (--log-probs-chunk-size -1), and sglang was reserving 66.5 GB of KV cache for a workload needing 7.3 GB. Memory is flat across rounds (14.40 → 26.00 → 26.00 → 26.01 GB), so none of this was ever a leak.

A clean exit is an upper bound on productive time, not a measure of it: a run can complete and still contribute nothing, and — as section 1 shows — several completed runs contributed a number that turned out to mean nothing.

    print()

The defect this session produced, and what caught it¶

Thirteen replacement runs were launched with N_SAMPLES, while the launcher reads N_SAMPLES_1P5B — the alias is applied one layer above the entry point the refill loop calls. All thirteen took the default n_samples = 1, where a GRPO group holds a single trajectory and the advantage is reward − reward = 0 exactly; the logs confirm 'rollout/advantages': 0.0 on every round. They would have completed, looked clean, and filled all four cells of the matrix with the same non-learning model.

What caught it was the [bsz] line added an hour earlier while fixing the global batch defect — a print whose only purpose was to make the resolved triple greppable. The value of printing a resolved configuration is not that you read it; it is that the next mistake in the same chain becomes visible without being looked for. The matrix collector now refuses any run whose logged n_samples disagrees with the cell its name claims.

12. What stands¶

  1. The 9B gradient pathology is real and total. 38 finite gradients across 24 runs, every one at least 2.5e7; the 1.5B on the same code sits between 0.0099 and 1.7e5. The distributions do not overlap.

  2. The nan originates in a full-attention layer. 64 of 64 diagnostic reports put the boundary on a layer in {3, 7, …, 31}. The Gated DeltaNet parameters that dominated the investigation for a week are downstream of it, and their being always-nan is what made them uninformative.

  3. It is not an overflow. 24 orders of headroom separate the largest finite gradient from fp32's limit, so the mechanism is a discrete non-finite event, not smooth growth. This distinction decides the fix: scaling repairs overflow and does nothing for 0*inf.

  4. No cell contrast in the 2×2 is currently established, and the cells are not even internally comparable. Every cell mixes two or three code states, because the shared checkout was edited while the matrix filled. Beyond that: The reward-form effect is +0.07 with a CI spanning zero. The group-size effect read +0.40 [+0.28, +0.52] before the refill, but it reverses at the shallowest truncation once newly started runs enter the pool, because a run's opening rounds have a high zero-variance rate while the GP is cold. And the cells it compared differed by 2× in optimiser steps, so even the pre-refill reading was measuring configuration and training budget together. The corrected launcher removes the second problem; only more runs at equal maturity remove the first.

  5. No claim about policy improvement has ever been testable on this pipeline, because the only outcome measure recorded falls on its own with the policy held fixed.
